samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Vincent Martin Hanrahan was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Amanda Daugherty
sp.p: I'm Amanda Daugherty, and I'm here with Veteran Vince Hanrahan. We have videographer Tim Grover and court reporter Bev Herring. Veteran Vince Hanrahan was born April 30th, 1924. He served in the United States Air Force in World War II, reached the rank of Lieutenant Colonel, and this interview is being conducted for the Veterans History Project at the Library of Congress. So, Vince, will you tell us a little bit about your background, where you were born, if you want to provide some family information and what you were doing before entering the service.

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: Okay. I was born in Des Moines; and my folks -- my father was an insurance salesman, life insurance; and my mother was a housewife with five kids. And my grandparents, I want to mention them: my grandmother came from Ireland when she was 16 years old -- and this is on my mother's side -- and my grandfather was a policeman on the Des Moines Police Department. His parents came from Ireland. He was born in this country. But my father was on the Des Moines Police Department from 1902 to 1917, when he passed away. Irish cop. So, on my father's side, those grandparents didn't come from Ireland, but their parents all did, so I guess I'm all Irish. And they were farmers; and about the time of World War I, they retired and moved to Des Moines. So, I was born here, went to school here. And I guess, might say my military career almost started on Pearl Harbor Day, December 7, 1941, when the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor. There were a bunch of us kids, we hung out, like kids do, at what's known as the Roosevelt Shopping Center right close to Roosevelt High School. December 7th, 1941 was -- 1941, that's right -- was a Sunday, and it was a real nice day for that time of year. So, we were all gathered at the Roosevelt Shopping Center, I suppose eight or ten of us guys, and had our car radios on, listening to the news. It was all about Pearl Harbor and what a terrible thing it was. So after we listened to that most of the day, we all decided we were going to go down in the morning and enlist. We were all about 17. So we all went home to tell our parents what our decision was and that we were going down to enlist the next morning in the service. Well, Monday morning, we all were at Roosevelt. We were 100 percent vetoed by our parents. None of them wanted us to go in the service at that time. So I finished school at Roosevelt, graduated that May or June, and still wanted to go in the service. My older brother was two years older than I was, and he had enlisted in the Air Force -- Air Corps it was back then. And as little brothers do, I wanted to do what my older brother did, so I wanted to go down and enlist in the Air Corps, and every time I'd bring it up, my parents would put the kibosh on the idea, and I understood that later on. My mother lost her only brother in World War I. He was killed in France. And my father was in the infantry in World War I. He served in France and saw a lot of service. So I understand it now, why they didn't want me to go to service. So I graduated from Roosevelt, and I went to work at Bankers Life. Bankers Life is a big insurance company here that -- and they had a program, what they called two-year boys, for boys that wanted to go on to college when they graduated from high school but didn't have the money, and I fit in there very well. So this nice lady on my paper route got me a job down there as a two-year boy working in the supply department, would send out supplies for the different agents around the country. But all the time, I wanted to be in the service; and every now and then, I'd bring it up and my parents would say no. So, finally, it got to be about November, and they realized that I was going to be going before long anyway. I'd turned 18 that April. So, finally, they gave in and said I could join the service. So I went down to the recruiting office in November, and lo and behold, they had frozen enlistments. The Navy, there were -- the Air Corps were all getting too many men, there weren't enough men for the draft. They were all going in where they wanted to go. So the only way you could get in was to volunteer to be drafted. So the man there at the enlisting office told me that. He said, "We have a form here that shows you came in and volunteered, and you take that, and they'll probably give you anything you want." Uh-huh, yeah. So I went to the draft board, and I told them I wanted to get in the service, and I had this thing, and I wanted to go to the Air Force -- Air Corps; and they looked at it, said, "That's real nice, real nice," so they started the paperwork to get me in the service; and they said I'd hear from them, and I did, in December. Had to go down and take some physicals and the usual thing. And they told me that I'd get orders in the mail when to report. It was just before Christmas, so they were kind enough to let me stay home for Christmas, but I was ordered to report to Camp Dodge in January. So I reported to Camp Dodge, and that's where I officially entered the service. It was January 26th, I believe. I was only there four or five days. We got our uniforms, did some more physicals and what have you. They stuck us on a troop train, and I'm sure I'm headed for some Air Force base someplace. We didn't know, have any idea where we were going, but this train kept going south for days, it seemed like. Finally, the train pulled up at the place called Camp Swift, Texas. It's right outside of -- excuse me -- it's right outside of Austin, Texas. And so we learned immediately that we were in the Corps of Engineers; so I got out my little paper and went up and showed the Lieutenant that I was supposed to be in the Air Corps, and he read it over and told me that was real nice, yeah. So, with this bunch of fellows that I came -- went down with from Camp Dodge were forming a new company, a river-crossing company. It was part of the Corps of Engineers. And what they'd do is go ahead of the infantry and build a bridge so the infantry could cross the river. It wasn't a very pleasant assignment. But every place I'd go, I'd show them this paper that I was supposed to be in the Air Corps, not in the Engineers; and they'd all read it, saying, "Isn't that nice? Yeah." So, finally, I got through to somebody -- oh. And the reason they put me in the Engineers is the experience I had working down at the home office of a big insurance company, had my occupation listed as supply -- supply clerk. So, as the supply sergeant, was going to go to officer's candidate school, and I was to take over and be the supply sergeant. And this was a brand-new company. It was just a cadre of a few officers and a few enlisted men and all these fellows from Camp Dodge. So we started basic training, and I want to tell you, basic training in the Corps of Engineers was no picnic. It seemed like we marched all day every day and all night every night. When we weren't marching, we were doing calisthenics and learning how to build bridges and how to set off dynamite and all that stuff. And every chance I got, I showed somebody my paper that I was supposed to be in the Air Corps. So, finally, I got through to somebody, and I got word I was to go to some air base nearby there and take a physical, see if I was qualified to get in the cadet program. And I did that, and I passed the physical. So I was slated to transfer to the Air Corps then finally. But in the meantime, I kept doing the basic training with the Engineers. And it was hard work, but I enjoyed it. I enjoyed it more than the other guys. They were all old men, 25, 26 years old; but I was young. I was 18. I could stand as long, march and things. So, after 13 weeks, we finished basic training, everybody was to get a furlough, come back home for 10, 12 days. And my lieutenant, who was just a real nice guy, strict but nice, said, "Hanrahan, you'll probably be transferring to the Air Corps, so I'm going to put you in with the first bunch to go on furlough." We couldn't all go at once, so just a small group would go and come back, another group would go. So I got to come home with the first group. And I was home for about 10 or 12 days, went back, and everybody was gone, everybody except one officer and a sergeant or two and a couple other guys to hold down the fort. What happened, there was a bad flood up in the state of Arkansas. Beings we were a river-crossing outfit, we had a lot of boats and bridge-building equipment, trucks and all that, they sent the whole company up there to help out with the flood. So, there were just a handful of us there with nothing to do, but they kept us busy. And before the company came back, I got orders to report to Shepard Field, and so I never did get to see those guys with the Corps of Engineers. And they were one real grand bunch of guys, I'll tell you, even though some of them were old guys, 25, 26 years old. I saw a few of them after the War. There were several of them from Des Moines, but... So I went to -- I've got to have some notes here, I was stationed in so many places. I went to -- I'm lost already, even with my notes. Okay. I went to Shepard Field and was there for -- oh, just a few days, and then they sent me to a terrible place called Xavier University in Cincinnati. You couldn't ask for any better than that. Xavier University is a Jesuit school, Catholic school, and run by the Jesuit priests that are all just brilliant. So I was there three months. They crammed about four years of college into three months. Then went back to the San Antonio Aviation Cadet Center, and I was there for what's called a preflight. That's like another basic training only ten times more rigorous. And they have lower class and upper class. The upper class would get to beat the lower classmen in, you know, things like making you scrub the floor, and it was just spotless, and the upperclassmen would come in and inspect it and say, "This floor is too dirty, scrub it again," you know, things like that that drive you crazy. But after you're halfway through, you're an upperclassman, then you get to do that to the new lower classmen coming in. And it was that way all the way through the cadet program, but -- it wasn't quite as rigorous after you got into the flying part of it, but... So, from preflight there in San Antone, I went to Vic- -- what was called Victory Field in Vernon, Texas. That's where I did my first flying. Well, not really my first flying. When I was with the Engineers in Austin, I thought somebody might pay more attention to my letter that says I'm supposed to go to the Air Corps if I got in a little flying experience. I'd never been up in an airplane, so whenever I would get to go to -- we'd get off base, I'd run out to the airport and take a flying lesson in a little old airplane. So for the first -- first flying for the Air Corps was just basically Victory Field in Vernon, Texas, and flying PT-19s, open cockpit. We were there three months, and that was quite an experience. About half of the guys washed out of pilot training, so they were gone. Then after primary training, I got sent to Enid, Oklahoma, air base there for bigger airplane, and flew the BT-13 there. It was a bigger plane, a more dangerous plane. Lost a lot of fellows. A lot of them spun in and got killed. A lot of them got washed out too. So that lasted three months. Then on to Enid Air Force Base at Enid, Oklahoma. That was advanced flying. It was in a twin-engine aircraft. So my goal was to be a fighter pilot. I wanted to fly one of those new P-51s, but I didn't have a letter that told me I should get preference on that, so I ended up in multi-engines. So -- did I say Enid, Oklahoma? That was basic. Went to Altus -- Altus, Oklahoma, for flying -- multi-engine flying. And after three months there, graduated on August 4th, 1944, got my pilot's wings, commissioned Second Lieutenant. So then we got a leave after graduation, so I got to come home for 10 or 12 days, but they gave us our assignment before we left. My assignment was to be an instructor at Miami, Florida. I really got a few good breaks. Only, when I was home on leave, I got orders telling me my orders had been changed; I was not to go to Miami; I was to go to Lincoln, Nebraska. So at the end of my leave, I went to Lincoln, Nebraska; and from there, I was sent out to Casper, Wyoming, and made a pilot, B-24 pilot. And so we trained there for three months, oh, formation flying, bombing and what you do in combat. Then we were to go to Topeka, Kansas, get ready to go overseas. Well, this was in December; and we were all sitting around, just waiting to get on the train to go to Topeka, Kansas. And shortly before that, we had one gunner on the crew that was a nice kid, but he couldn't stay out of trouble. He was real funny and happy-going, but he was always getting in trouble. And, finally, they decided he wasn't right to go overseas, so they jerked him off the crew. While we were sitting around, waiting to get on this train, the Sergeant came in -- and, oh, by the way, I was just sicker than a dog this day. I don't know why, but -- I'd never been so sick in my life. I was sitting around, waiting for the -- to get on this train, the Sergeant came down, he said, "We got word from Topeka, Kansas, no crews are to be sent there unless they're a full crew." They didn't want to have to replace anybody there. So they said, "You guys will stay here and your new gunner will be here next week and we'll put you on a plane and fly you down." Okay. "Take me to the hospital. I'm dying. I know I'm dying." So they loaded me in an old car that was kept on the base there to kick around in. Took me up to the hospital. I wasn't in the hospital five minutes till they had me in the operating room doing surgery on me. I had an appendix that was just about to break. So they took my appendix out. Now, you know, if you go to the hospital and have surgery, they expect you to get up off the operating table and walk back to the room. Well, back then, if you had any surgery that was serious at all, they made you lie on your back in bed for 30 days, couldn't get out of bed. About halfway through, they'd let you what they call dangle. You could sit on the edge of the bed and let your legs dangle. So I was lying in that bed for all of that time. The other guys, they couldn't go to Topeka because they didn't have a full crew. So it was getting close to Christmas, and they decided they'd rather be home for Christmas than sitting around in Casper, Wyoming. So they went to the Red Cross; the Red Cross said, yeah, they could see if they got leave; so they fixed them all up, even drew the orders; and the guy that drew the orders made a mistake and put my name on it too. I hadn't been out of this bed for a couple weeks. I could hardly -- I knew I wasn't going to be able to stand up, but I wasn't going to pass up a chance to be home for Christmas, so I didn't tell them they made a mistake. I just went along with them and came home for Christmas. I was weak, I could hardly get on and off the train, but it was well worth it. So then -- Don't you have any questions?

sp.speaker: Amanda Daugherty
sp.p: I think the next thing is, kind of tell me about, you know, what your wartime service was like and going overseas.

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: Okay. And I'm not even up there.

sp.speaker: Amanda Daugherty
sp.p: You can go ahead and finish through, if you want.

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: Okay. Well, if you have a question for me, let me know.

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: So, we went back to Topeka and got all our equipment and stuff, and we got a brand-new B-24 airplane. It was right off the assembly line. And, boy, there's a difference between an old airplane and a brand-new one: it's faster, it's safer, you can depend on everything to work. So we flew this new airplane to New Hampshire, spent the night there; and from there, we were to fly to Bermuda and on to the Azores; so -- another one of my good breaks -- so we flew to New Hampshire, spent the night and then jumped off to Bermuda. When we got to Bermuda, it was January, and the Atlantic gets pretty rough in the wintertime, in January. There was a terrible storm out in the Atlantic, so they weren't sending any planes on to Europe. They were all sitting there. So this island was just covered with planes. We could hardly find a place to park our plane, but we had to spend all this time on Bermuda, waiting for the weather to clear up out over the Atlantic. Wonderful. Nothing to do but ride a bicycle around the island all day long. So we were there about 10 days. Then, finally, the Weather Bureau or the weathermen decided the storm had cleared up enough that it was safe to start sending these planes off. There wasn't any room for any more on the island as it was. So they're sending them off. They're staggering them quite a bit, because there's still some weather out there. They said, "Don't worry about it, you'll be able to climb up over to 16,000 feet, and you won't hit it until about three hours out." So about two hours out, we hit the storm; and we climbed as high as that brand-new B-24 would go, about 25,000 feet, and it didn't clear up at all. It was a terrible storm. We were flying upside down more than we were flying right-side up. In fact, the guys that were gunners and men that were sitting back in the back end of the plane said that they actually spent more time hanging onto the ceiling than they did the floor all the time. And this went on and on and on. And here are all these other airplanes out there, you don't know who you're going to run into. So that was a terrible experience. I think it was about a 10- or 11-hour flight. Finally, we got to the Azores and then landed, and I was so tired from fighting that airplane all night long, I went into the tent and I -- I never slept so long in all my life. We were there for overnight. I spent all that time asleep. So -- and it was a bad storm. We'd look up, a plane would be coming in, and it would have maybe half its rudder torn off or the bomb bay door torn off. So, the next day, we flew on to Tunis, Tunisia, and spent a couple days there; then flew up to someplace in Italy -- I don't remember where it was -- one of the bigger towns; and up there, they gave us our assignment. I was assigned -- our crew was assigned to the 450th Bomb Group that was stationed down in Manduria, Italy, which was down in the heel of the boot as far south as anybody was stationed in Italy. So they gave us equipment, took our brand- new airplane away from us and gave us an old junker that had more missions on it than anybody. So we flew that old plane down to Manduria and became officially part of the 450th Bomb Group, 27- -- 721st Bomb Squadron. And so from there, we flew missions. Every crew wouldn't fly every day, but every second or third day, you'd get a mission. Most of our missions were up into Germany or Austria, up in that part of Europe, so some were very long ones. And this was getting along in April, and the -- our intelligence found out -- the War was going bad for Germany. We were just chasing them all over the place, and Hitler had a pretty good idea he was going to lose this war. So our intelligence found out that Hitler put out the word that when it was evident that there was just no way he could win that war, all the prisoners of war would be killed that were being held in Germany; so they wanted volunteers -- they mapped out this program what they were going to do to save these POW's, so they wanted volunteers to fly out and bail out near these POW camps, go down and be taken a prisoner and be taken into that camp so you'd know what the program was and you could get the guys in the camp organized. So who volunteered? You know, right now, I can look back and think, my gosh, why would anybody volunteer, bail out and be taken prisoner in a camp where they're going to shoot everybody? But it was no big deal then, and they had no trouble getting volunteers. A lot of the guys volunteered. We had plenty of volunteers. So I got a little tied up in that program, had to go to a lot of briefings and things, didn't fly as often as I would otherwise. In fact, I hadn't flown for a week, hadn't gone on a mission for a week. And it was April 8th when I flew again, and the mission that day was a railroad bridge up in Brander Pass; and everything went off fine until we got on the bomb run over this bridge; and then the Germans opened up with that flack; and the sky was black with it, it looked like you could get out and walk on it. We took a hit in the inboard engine on the right side, and it knocked us right out of formation. Then we got another hit on the outboard engine on the right side. A B-24 doesn't fly real well with four good engines, but when you take away two of them on the same side, you've got a job. So we were going down. We finally got the plane straightened out. Of course we were out of the formation as far as that goes. We could not fly back south in the shape we were in because of the mountains. We'd have to clear all those mountains; and the way that plane was going down, we couldn't clear those mountains. And we couldn't bail out, because there was nothing down there but mountains and snow, and it would just be suicide to try to bail out down there. And besides, the radio operator had taken a real good hit right in his knee. His knee was shot away. He couldn't bail out. So it was decided the only sensible thing to do was to cut across Switzerland and find a friendly field in France -- and we had most of France by then, not all of it -- and try somehow to get that plane landed in France. So we headed out over Switzerland, but when we got into Switzerland, we were jumped by three Swiss fighters. They were ME-109s, Messerschmitts, Germany's best fighter plane. And the pilots let us know that we were to follow them down or they'd shoot us down, so they led us over to this little fighter strip. The runways in Italy were 9,000 feet long. We usually used every foot of it, especially if we had a bomb load. And that little fighter strip that -- the strip looked like it was about a block long, but we didn't have any choice. It was either go down and try it or these fighter pilots would take us down. So we went down, landed and used every foot of the runway, right on the tip of the runway. Then the trick was to get the nose wheel down so we'd get on the brakes and get that thing stopped before it ran out of that runway. Well, beautiful landing. Hit the nose wheel down. As soon as the nose wheel came down -- the nose wheel had been hit, and we didn't know that; and as soon as it went down, it pulled it back up. The plane just literally crashed then. So, the next thing I knew was, when the dust finally settled, look up, and there were all these soldiers around us in uniforms just like the German soldiers wore, the dark green, the bucket helmets the Germans wore; and they were jabbering in German, shouting at us in German, and each one of them had a rifle sticking right in our face. And the Germans had a trick of setting up air bases just inside Germany, near Switzerland, putting Swiss marks -- markings on them. Our planes get in trouble, have to go down, they'd go down and land on these bases and be taken prisoners. So we thought we were in Switzerland for a couple days -- or, in Germany, rather. Excuse me. But they put us up at a -- it was an officers' school there, and that was nice. They had all kinds of groceries. We even had wine on the table at dinnertime. And they kept trying to tell us we were in Switzerland, but we didn't know. There was a nice guy, a Swiss officer, claimed he went to college in the United States. I don't doubt it, because he knew more about the United States than any of us. But, of course, we realized all the time he was pumping us for information. We'd tell him a lot of things, they were all lies, but he probably knew it too. So we were there for a couple days, and they shipped us off to a -- up in the mountains, a little town called Adelboden. It was a resort town. Had a couple hotels, and that was all it was. Ski -- ski trails. And shortly before that, there had been an agreement between Switzerland, Germany and the United States. There were about 600 Americans up there, prisoners with the Swiss. They worked out this agreement that they'd release all the Americans, release so many Germans -- I think we finally agreed to releasing two Germans for every one American. Anyway, they emptied the place out. So the day we went in there, nobody was in there. Two nice hotels -- or, they had been nice hotels. They hadn't been used, except for the prisoners, for years. So, they put us up there because there was this road up to it, this little town; and on this side of the road, it went straight up as far as you could see; and this side, it went straight down as far down as you could see. The only way you could get up there was go up this road. So the Swiss just set up a guardhouse there. No way you could come down out of that town without going by this guardhouse. So, like I say, it was nice, beaut- -- the mountains were beautiful, and the Swiss pilots would come up there and show off. They'd fly down below us. We could look down on the top of the airplane, and they'd fly down and do their acrobatics and show off. So the only thing bad about it, other than being out of the war -- I know that's hard to understand, but -- there wasn't any food. So they'd go out every day and pull some weeds and boil it in water and tell us it was soup, and that's what we lived on the time we were there. And, fortunately, we weren't there very long. But, you know, the number one rule for a prisoner of war is escape. You have a duty to escape, no matter what else. So, every -- not every night -- about every second or third night, we'd have one guy escape. And they -- In this hotel, there was one nice, big front doorway; and this Swiss guard would come and wheel his bed out, and he'd put it right against the door. That's where he slept. The only way you could get out of that hotel at night was to climb over him in bed, he thought. He didn't know Americans. Each room had a balcony on it. You could swing down on the balcony and swing into the balcony down below and get away. So every night or two, one of the guys would go out. And when they'd come to this guardhouse on the road down there, they'd have to go way down and -- straight down. Had to be a mountain goat almost to get out of there and to get around that guardhouse and then to walk across Switzerland into France. And the guard, he'd put his bed up against the door, then he'd go around and do bed check. Well, we had about three or four -- three or four floors we were using. And he'd go up and count the guys in bed on the second floor; then he'd go up to the next floor; and while he was going up to the next floor, the guys would get out of the bed on the fourth floor and go up the back steps and fill in the beds above him, so they'd do that so that every bed would be full by the time he got there, and so he never knew that we were slipping somebody out of there about every night. So that was on April the 8th that we went into Switzerland. Oh, I'll tell you this. You won't believe this. We're sitting around this hotel up in this little town, in the hotel where they kept us; and, like I say, there were about 30 men went in the day we went in, three crews. Then another day, another crew would come in that bailed out or crashed in Switzerland or something. And this one night after we'd been there about a week or two, they brought in a crew, and I looked up, there was a kid I went to high school with, Dick Manbeck, from Des Moines. And he wasn't in my class, he was a couple classes older; but his sister, Barbara Manbeck, was in my class, so I knew him quite well. And if you can imagine the odds of that happening, so Dick and I became real good friends. So then the War ended in May in Europe. And Switzerland decided that they had to keep ahold of us prisoners until the War ended in Japan. And the United States told them, no, they were wrong, they had to turn us loose, so they had a big fight over that. Well, you know who won: the United States won. So they turned us over to the Americans, but -- and they -- oh, they took us on a train. I don't remember where to, but the United States Air Force -- Air Corps picked us up and flew us up from France up to Le Havre. And up on Le Havre, they had all these camps where they were bringing in the -- all prisoners of war from all over Europe, and they had these different tent camps set up, and there's a Camp Lucky Strike, Camp Chesterfield, and they were named after cigarettes. So we went up there. Well, they could bring in these guys faster than they could put them on boats and send them back to this country, so it was real crowded. To make things worse, we were there for -- and our boat, I understand it was the biggest transport the Army had, the U.S.S. General Butner. It was a big transport. But it was just about to Le Havre to pick us up and it had boiler trouble, had to go back to England and get a new boiler. Kind of like this cruise ship that got stranded last week. So we spent more time in that camp, and there was nothing to do but every day walk down to the beach, and the beach was covered with -- oh, broken-down tanks and all kinds of things that you expect in a war and bombs sitting over there that didn't go off. So that was -- that was quite an experience. But, let's see, I thought of something else a minute ago I wanted to tell you. Oh, the attitude towards -- of the Swiss. Up in this little town, they were used to having Americans around, because there had been so many of the guys there before we got there, so they were very friendly, and of course they were making money off of them. We could wire home and have money sent to us, so we had lots of money. We didn't have to go hungry, but the black market, I think what we'd pay for a Swiss, a cheese sandwich would probably be about -- in today's dollars would be about $60 or $70 for a cheese sandwich, so we really weren't that hungry. But just a few weeks before we went in there, on April 8th, there was a big raid on Germany. Now, it was the 8th Air Force, and Italy was the 15th Air Force, two different Air Forces. I was in the 15th. The 8th was in England. You probably heard a lot more about them than you did the 15th Air Force. They had a big raid on Germany on the -- in Germany, but the weather was real bad; so when they took off from England, they decided not to group up until they got over France, which they did. And then they got over to Germany where they were going to do the bombing, and it was just solid clouds from the ground to way up, so they decided to scrap the mission, go back to England, take their bombs home with them. Well, when they made the turn in all these clouds, six different -- well, several planes got separated out of formation; and there were six planes flying around up there trying to find the rest of the planes where they belonged up above the clouds, and they -- they were from different groups. Three of them were from one group, two of them were from one group, and the sixth one was from another group. So they had got together in formation for their own protection in case they got jumped by fighters. They were looking around, trying to find their -- the other planes and couldn't find them. They finally saw a hole in the clouds, and they determined that it was a little town -- I can't remember the name of it -- a little German town, and they couldn't see much of the whole town anyway through this hole, but they decided it would be a good place to leave their bombs. Nobody likes to land with a full load of bombs. That's very dangerous. So these six planes went down through this hole and bombed this town. And they bombed a lot of houses and some buildings and killed I think about six people and injured a lot more, flew on back to England. And the next day, if you're looking at the -- they had photos of the bomb strikes of the town; and when the intelligence was going over the pictures, the photos, they decided that couldn't be the town they thought it was; and they studied these pictures and determined it was Zurich, Switzerland, they had bombed. About 48,000 pounds on Zurich. So the Swiss people had remembered that when we got there, and they were not happy with us at all because of that. In fact, every time this train that was taking us up in the mountains would stop, they'd all come out and throw rocks at the train. And I guess you can't blame them. So, anyway, our boat finally got to us in France, at Le Havre, and came home on the boat. And it was -- it was a big boat, you know. You'd think it would hold the whole United States Army, but it was crowded, guys sleeping on the decks and what have you. But we -- we got to Newport News, happy to be back in the United States; and we were sent to Jefferson Barracks; and from there, got a leave, got to come home to Des Moines. And the Army had a procedure. If you went to your doctor and the doctor would try to give you a letter that said he thought you needed a little more time at home to get back together, so, of course, that's what I did, that's what everybody did, and I got an extended leave, so I was home for a long time that summer, and I was in Des Moines when the War ended in Japan. So, then, after that leave was over, I went back to San Antonio, a different base, to be discharged. Well, I elected to stay in the Air Corps Reserves. Several guys did. So I stayed in the Reserve for -- well, for 19- -- 1984, I believe, was the date of my -- I was finally kicked out. And I had an interesting time in the Reserve. When I first got out, there were a lot of pilots that stayed in the Reserve, guys that I'd gone to school with, my friends; and we could call over to Offutt Air Force Base and say, "We've got some Reserve pilots over here, and we'd like to do some flying tomorrow. Could you come over and pick us up?" "Sure." So they'd send a transport over here and pick us up at the Des Moines Airport, fly us over to Offutt. And they had about every kind of airplane known to man over there. You could fly anything you want, just go up to get your flying time in. So we'd fly around for the day and come back to Offutt, they'd fly us back to Des Moines, and that was great. We'd just do it whenever we wanted to. And they were real nice to us over at Offutt. But then the government decided they were wasting too much money letting these guys go have their joy rides, so they put a stop to that, and -- but I was still in the Reserve, would go to meetings every Tuesday night, I think it was, out at -- out at Fort Des Moines here. And then I got the letter from the Pentagon -- Oh. In the meantime, I'd gone to Drake, finished college, then went through law school and became a lawyer. In 1950, I graduated, became a lawyer. So it's about 1955, I got this letter from the Pentagon that they wanted to establish a Reserve Judge Advocate General's group in Des Moines and would I help them with it. Sure. So I formed this group, and I was the commander of this group. It was a very, very small group of guys that stayed in the Reserve and were lawyers. And it was a small group, but the Navy had a Judge Advocate General's Reserve group here that was larger, so I made arrangements we'd meet with them, and it worked out real well. And we had such a small group, it didn't -- because there weren't many lawyers that was reservists in the Army, so that kind of fell by the wayside, but I was still going to my meetings out here at Camp Dodge. And then I was approached by a -- it was what was called a recovery group. You probably never heard of such a thing, but what a recovery group was -- remember, there was a cold war going on back then. If the United States should be attacked and, like I say, they'd bomb Offutt Field, all these planes would be up in the air, shooting at whoever they were shooting at, wouldn't have anyplace to go back and land. They had to go someplace. This recovery group would set up a place for them to come to. And they asked me if I'd come and be their -- be the Administrative Officer of this group, which was fine. I liked that. So we had I think it was five squadrons around the state. We had one in Ottumwa, one in Waterloo. I don't remember where all they were, but we were over them. We were at Fort Des Moines. And the idea of the thing was, they wouldn't have a lot of equipment, but they'd contact -- like, we'd contact the big contractors in Des Moines and get an agreement with them that if this ever happened, they'd turn over so many bulldozers, trailers, gas trucks, whatever we needed to them voluntarily; and we had it right down to even who was going to feed the guys. And we did have our own fire truck out there, you know. It was an old Army fire truck, and we had that thing shined up. And we had a generator. It was -- oh, about twice the size of this room. I think you could supply electricity for the city of Des Moines forever with that big generator we had. We had a lot of silly stuff like that that the Army didn't need, so they just sent it to us. So I was in that group for a long time. The only bad part about it, sometimes you'd get a call at 3 o'clock in the morning, you didn't know whether we had really been invaded or it was just another drill. You had to get up and get out to the fort and maybe run down to Ottumwa or up to Waterloo or someplace. And you always had to have what we called a go-away kit with you, a suitcase with some uniforms and shaving gear and all that so in case you got called away, and so I kept mine in the trunk of my car. And you always had to -- had to be someone that knew where you were. If you went on vacation, you had to make arrangements. And the only other bad thing about it -- it really wasn't a bad thing; I didn't mind it -- being a Group Administration Officer, I was in charge of all the restricted material, so whenever a top-secret piece of information come in out at the fort, I had to drop whatever I was doing and run out there and sign for it, get it locked in the big safe where the restricted stuff was. I was the only guy that could get in that safe. So there were -- there were -- it did take a lot of time; but, meantime, I'm building up all these points for my retirement. So, finally, I retired as Lieutenant Colonel after 41 years of service. Oh, and when I was Adminis- -- Group Administration Officer, they called us into the Pentagon for about a week of active duty one time. And while they were there, they treated us like kings. They took us over to the United States Supreme Court, and we were all admitted to practice in the United States Supreme Court. Took us over to the Court of -- United States Court of Military Appeals, and we were sworn in over there, so was able to practice before that court, so that was a good experience. And we got -- went on active duty every summer for a week or two, two or three days at a time, so it built up a lot of time. So the Cold War kind of went away, and they didn't see much need for recovery groups anymore, they did away with that. After several years of doing that, went back, going to my meetings out there, and so I stayed in until 1984. Don't regret it. So that was the end of my military career.

sp.speaker: Amanda Daugherty
sp.p: Thank you for sharing your story. Are there any life lessons that you've learned that you would like to share with us?

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: Oh, one thing. When I was in the service, I don't know how many thousands of men I met, you know, all the different places, different things I did, thousands and thousands, I never met a one man -- they were all men then -- I never met one man I didn't like, who wasn't what I'd call a real good guy. So I learned that basically people are good.

sp.speaker: Amanda Daugherty
sp.p: That's great. I guess, do you remember, when you returned home from being overseas, what was that homecoming like?

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: Oh, that was great. Go in a bar, you couldn't buy a beer. You had them sitting up in front of you. Everybody wanted to buy you a bar -- buy you a beer. And, in Des Moines, there weren't any bases around here except the WACS, lady soldiers, so there was a lot of extra ladies in Des Moines. All the guys -- all the guys were off in the service, so, man, I probably didn't have a lot of trouble getting dates in high school, but I sure didn't have any trouble when I was home on leave. So...

sp.speaker: Amanda Daugherty
sp.p: Do you still have contact with fellow veterans?

sp.speaker: Videographer
sp.p: Excuse me. I've got about six minutes left on the tape.

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: Oh, okay. Not -- not guys I was in the service with. It seems like so many of them have died, you know. Of course, a long time after the War, I'd correspond with a lot of them, but they were spread all over, and so, gradually, they faded away, I guess.

sp.speaker: Vincent Martin Hanrahan
sp.p: No. I just want to thank you all and thank everybody that put on this program out here today. I know it took a lot of work to do it, and I surely do appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Amanda Daugherty
sp.p: Thank you. Thank you for your service and for participating in this Veterans History Day Project. Today is November 11th, 2010, and this was conducted in Des Moines, Iowa. Thank you very much. (Close of the record at 10:00 a.m. on November 11, 2010.)
